verdict: OK to lend in Surat dyeing and processing, but only to units with clean labour compliance and verified effluent/waste handling; avoid units with unresolved wage disputes or no PLI-linked upgrade plan.
title: Surat textile dyeing & processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A dyeing and processing house takes grey fabric or yarn, runs it through wet processes (scouring, dyeing, finishing) using boilers, effluent treatment and power, and sells finished fabric to garmenters and traders. **Cash is made on throughput and colour/quality consistency, not on the machine.** The two biggest cash sinks are power and water/effluent treatment, plus the working-capital cycle of holding inventory and carrying receivables [8]. So when a proposal lands, check the power source and the effluent plant first; if either is outsourced or informal, ask who bears the cost and the compliance risk.

## Where value and cash sit now
Value sits with units that can upgrade machinery and hold quality, and the PLI revision just widened that door: minimum investment cut from ₹100 crore to ₹50 crore and turnover from ₹200 crore to ₹100 crore, with an 11% first-year incentive tapering to 7% by year five [1]. **That is the growth lever for mid-size Surat processors.** But the same unit faces a labour cost reset: workers are demanding eight-hour shifts, overtime after that, a 48-hour week cap and double wages for overtime under the amended Factories Act, and a fresh protest was called for November 1 after August unrest [3]. So when a proposal lands, check the wage register against the amended Act; if overtime is unpaid or shifts run 12 hours, ask for the remediation plan before sanctioning [2][3].

## The growth opportunity to pursue
Pursue mid-size processors with a credible PLI Part-II plan — ₹50 crore investment and ₹100 crore turnover now qualify — and a clean labour record [1]. **Peer results show the upside is real but uneven:** Arvind's Q2 FY27 net profit rose 44% to ₹148 crore on 23% revenue growth to ₹2,919 crore [6], while Sportking's operating margin jumped to 19% in Q1 FY27 from 12% a year earlier, though its three-year profit CAGR was -8% [7]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the margin is from power cost (Sportking's 40.3 MW solar could add ₹14-16 crore annually [7]) or from a one-off; if it is one-off, ask for the sustainable margin.

## How to grow safely
Structure term loans against the PLI capex with milestone disbursement tied to machinery commissioning, and keep working-capital limits sized to the actual inventory-and-receivable cycle [8][9]. **Take every month:** GST returns, wage and overtime registers, effluent plant logs, and power bills. If GST collections in Gujarat are running +11.9% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], that is a local tailwind, but it does not fix a unit with unpaid overtime. Avoid units with unresolved wage disputes or no effluent compliance; the Extended Bulk Waste Generator framework now forces on-site wet-waste processing or compliance certificates [4], so ask for the certificate.

## Early-warning signs
Watch for a strike call or FIR at the unit — August unrest led to three FIRs and 26 detentions [3] — and treat any repeat as a stop signal. **Watch the wage register monthly:** if overtime hours exceed the 125-per-quarter cap without double pay, the unit is one dispute away from a shutdown [3]. Watch power cost per metre and effluent penalties; if either jumps, ask for the cause before renewing the limit. Note that sources say little specific to Surat dyeing beyond the PLI and labour news, so lean on first principles and the peer margin data [6][7].
